A request names its model in its body's `Model:` field; adoption re-reads it,
**gates it on the issue author's push access** (the body is author-editable
where a label was write-gated, so an ungated author's ask still runs — at the
default, never automerged), and the session runs at it. That is the **first time an item carries
anything behavior-defining**, so it is fenced rather than waved through:

- Only a task that declares `model_from_request: true` reads it — one task does, and
  it is engine-owned, so no pack can opt itself in.
- The value is validated against the model families; anything else falls back to the
  declared default rather than failing, and the run says on the issue which model it
  actually used. It is re-read and re-gated at every adoption (§16.3), so only the
  pending ask's choice ever routes a run — a stale value from an earlier ask
  cannot outrank a new one.
- The trust argument: the field is honored only when the issue **author** holds
  push access — read from the collaborators-permission API at the same place
  the marker's permission is read (§16.4), never `author_association` — and the
  mark that arms the run is still platform-write-gated. A drive-by author on a
  public repo can write any body they like; what they get is the default model
  and no automerge.

The rejected alternative was one task per family (three near-identical folders,
routed by label) — it keeps `agent_model` purely in tracked files, and it was what
the pack cut did, but three copies of one task in the engine to avoid one guarded
field is the worse trade. *(Owner, 2026-08-19: keep the field.)*

### 16.8 What this does not change

Ceilings, exec records, the claim lease, heartbeats, the janitor's rules, the triage
lanes and which of them hold a task's lane, capacity, the `after` yield, suspension
(`CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL` freezes adoption with everything else), and dormancy
(a dormant repo adopts nothing — marks simply wait). A request item is picked,
arbitrated and recovered by the same code as any other item, which is the point.

### 16.9 Rejected alternatives

- **A pack** (the first cut, 2026-08-18). It could not reach the scheduler run, so it
  re-implemented adoption as an hourly precondition over labels plus a worker that
  authorized, picked and label-swapped — a second dispatch mechanism living beside
  the queue, with the model spent as three task folders. Rejected by the owner on
  sight; this section is the correction.
- **Authorization in code-work.** Workable (a worker holds the token) but it puts a
  run/no-run decision after the single evaluation site, which is the one thing §6.4
  forbids.
- **Task-less request items** — an item shape the executor special-cases. It saves
  the built-in-task plumbing and costs every downstream guard a branch: validation,
  ceiling, records and instructions all grow "unless it is a request".

input.title: Label scheme PRs 1–2: decode every spelling, and the marked issue becomes the item
input.body:
#1119's review pass, **stages 1 and 2**, as two separate commits on one branch — this session may only push to its designated branch, so the plan's stacked-PR shape collapsed into one PR. Say the word and I will split stage 2 onto its own branch based on this one.

**PR 3 (the write-side flip) is deliberately not here**: the plan gates its merge on the fleet force that happens *after* 1–2 merge, so landing it beside them would jump that gate.

## Stage 1 — the read side + the stubs (commit `eef03a4`)

Additive on every member, in any order: **nothing writes a canonical status yet**.

- **One decode pass.** `work-item.mjs` gains the canonical vocabulary (`STATUS_*`, `ORIGIN_*`) and `statusOf` / `statusesOn` / `isParked` / `parkKindOf` / `originOf`. Every legacy spelling in DESIGN §4's table maps straight to today's, in one pass; a park whose kind cannot be decoded — an older engine's bare `needs-human`, a word a newer engine invents — reads as `failure`, the lane that holds the task's lane. No reader compares a label literally any more.
- **Transitions leave a status, not a label.** New `apply-status.mjs`: leaving a status clears *every* spelling of it, so an item filed as `task:ready` and picked up by an engine writing the canonical spelling cannot end up wearing two live statuses. The flip is then six constants changing. Side effect worth naming: a hand wake now clears the park's sub-label too, which it previously left standing.
- **The ensure-list carries the canonical labels already** — GitHub 422s an attempt to apply a label that does not exist, and the ensure pass reaches a member a converge before the flip does.
- **Both stubs, and the canon's own copies.** The executor triggers on `task:status:waiting-for-executor` *and* `task:ready` (and `task:urgent`) — a workflow's event trigger names label strings literally, so this is the one surface where both vocabularies must appear at once. Both workflows file their failure issues as `task:origin:github` + `task:status:needs-human-failure`, ensuring those labels first.

## Stage 2 — one-issue requests (commits `e2b5541`, `6e6529b`)

The shadow work item is gone. A person marks an ordinary issue `task:origin:ad-hoc`; adoption appends the machine block to **that issue's own body** and applies the first status; the lifecycle plays out where the person is already looking.

- **One lever.** Any status — live, parked or terminal — holds the mark until somebody clears it. No prior item to wait on, none to supersede; an impatient re-ask mid-run is structurally nothing.
- **Parameters ride the person's text**, not labels: `Task:`, `Model:`, `Automerge:`, beside `Blocked-by:` and `Not-before:`. Re-read at every adoption and honoured only for an author with push access, read from the collaborators-permission API — never the payload's association. An ungated ask still runs, at the defaults, and the adoption comment says so.
- **`Task: <pack>/<task>` is new** — which task a mark asks for, defaulting to the built-in implementer. An id this repo does not carry is not adopted at all: the mark waits. Recorded as DESIGN §16.12, since §16 only sketched it.
- **Nothing closes somebody's issue.** A refusal's terminal status stands on the open issue — the run's verdict is not the issue's validity — and so does the approval park, which *is* the in-review state.
- **Identity without a title**: a marked issue's task comes from the worker path its machine block names (`taskIdFromPath`). That closed two holes — the janitor's stale-ready rule skipped every request run, and the dashboard rendered them as belonging to no task.
- **Legacy is read forever**: `claude-task` still marks (and adoption gives the issue today's origin), and a draining shadow item still writes back to the issue it names.

## Findings for the plan

- **The stubs are converge-delivered, not copied-once** — `convergeWiring` rewrites both workflow files from the vendored stubs whole. Execution step 1's contingency does not apply. The lag is that `.github/workflows/` lands as a PR somebody merges, so a member spends a window on the old copy — costing a label event, never work, since the hourly scheduler dispatch is the guaranteed delivery. That window is now a rehearsal shape.
- **`consumer-safe-change` watched only the scheduler stub.** The executor's is vendored just as verbatim and its trigger is exactly the surface a vocabulary change must carry members across, so the check (canon-local) now covers both.
- **Left out of stage 2, deliberately**: folding `add-packs` into the `Task:` field. It rewrites a cross-repo contract (the enforcer writes into members over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`), and its real failure mode needs a decision — a member whose mark label does not exist yet refuses the enforcer's write, and nothing runs, where the current dispatch-and-wake protocol is robust to that. Everything the fold needs on this side is now in place.

## Folders touched

```
engine/scheduler/queue/       the decode + apply-status; the machine block and the
                              request-side field parse; adoption rewritten to write
                              onto the marked issue; executor/converge identity and
                              the never-close rule; the built-in task and its doc
engine/scheduler/signals/     the request read accepts either mark
engine/scheduler/stubs/       both workflow stubs — the executor's dual trigger, and
.github/workflows/            the canon's own hand-maintained copies of the same two
packs/basics/                 the janitor's queue sweep decodes; do-later and
                              verify-in-production speak the mark and the body fields
packs/claudinite-dashboard/   item state, triage, parked counts and item membership
vendoring/rehearsal/          the old-workflows fixture gains the pre-#1119 executor
docs/tasks-dispatch/          DESIGN §16.12 — the `Task:` targeting field
.claudinite/local/packs/…     consumer-safe-change now watches both stubs
```

- **One PR for the whole work list**, and **link both ways**: the PR body names the issue(s), and you comment the PR link on each. The fleet's weekly sweep closes them on its own once the declaration carries the packs; your comment is what makes the intervening week legible.

## 3. Report

Close out on your work item as usual: the packs adopted with the PR link, the packs declined with the reason, and anything left for a human — an adoption blocked on an unanswerable interview question is exactly that, and naming it is the whole handoff.

- **Never merge.** Open the PR and leave it for review.

## The fan-out model

Both stages end the same way, per member with work ([`protocol.mjs`](protocol.mjs)):

1. **Converge one work-list issue in that member** under the `add-packs` label — `Add packs: requested for this repo` (a decision, carrying the exact declaration entries as JSON, config and answers included) or `Add packs: suspected from this repo’s shape` (a suspicion, carrying the evidence and the fingerprints the REST sweep could not decide).
2. **Wake that member's own `adopt-requested-packs` item** by dispatching its scheduler with `wake: adopt-requested-packs`. The wake lever names one task and touches nothing else (engine contract, #749).

The member's task reads its own issue, its own executor confirms/adopts with the repo checked out, and one reviewed PR lands *there*. The enforcer **dispatches**; the member **executes**. Nothing here writes to any member's tree, and no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access — the one fleet credential is `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`, granted as [`fleet-token.mjs`](../../fleet-token.mjs) states it.

## Convergence

- A **requested** issue closes `completed` once the member's declaration carries everything its JSON block asks for — checked on every weekly visit, whichever run opened it.
- A **suspected** issue closes `completed` once the member declares the packs (or its shape stops suggesting them), and a `not planned` close is a standing decline the scan honours rather than re-suggesting weekly.
- A member with a still-open work list is **re-fired** on the weekly visit — the retry loop for a member whose earlier adoption run died.

## Failure is loud

A member that could not be swept is `unknown` — never "fitted" — and a member whose scheduler workflow refused the wake dispatch (missing workflow, PAT without Actions write, workflow disabled) is a work list nobody will act on. Both are named in the summary and fail the run; the executor converges the item to `needs-human`.

git add -A && git status --short && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Fold add-packs onto the marked issue

A member's add-packs work list was a labelled issue plus a `wake:` dispatch that
told the member's scheduler to run a task which then went looking for that issue.
The work list is a marked issue now: the enforcer applies `task:origin:ad-hoc`
and names the member task in the body's `Task:` field, so the member's own
scheduler run adopts it and the issue becomes the item the agent runs on.

What goes with the dispatch: the member task's code-work gate and its worker,
which existed only because a woken standing item had no idea why it was awake.
What stays: the label, the two converged titles, and the JSON block — the
protocol both sides still read.

Three things the fold has to get right, and does. The mark is created in the
member before it is applied, since a refused label is a work list nobody runs. A
re-forced ask keeps the machine block the member wrote and clears the status,
which is the sanctioned re-ask. And a second work list in a member names the
first in `Blocked-by:` — two lists are two items of one task, which nothing else
serializes, and two sessions on one declaration is two conflicting PRs.

The dispatch that remains is latency, not delivery: an ordinary scheduler run so
the mark is adopted in a minute rather than at the next hour, and a member that
refuses it is reported rather than failing the sweep.

Refs #1119
EOF

Write the canonical spellings

The flip. The constants every writer already uses now hold today's spellings, so
one edit moves every write site at once: statuses, terminals, and the origin the
generator, the hand-created item and the marked issue each wear for life. Their
NAMES survive because fielded pack versions import them — a pack still on the old
engine writes a legacy label, which every decoder here reads as what it meant.

A park stops being a pair. `needs-human` plus a sub-label could be half-applied,
which was a torn state of its own; a park is one `task:status:needs-human-<kind>`
now, written by one swap. The dashboard, which grouped the pair into a column,
gets its own display key for that column rather than borrowing a label nothing
writes.

The legacy spellings become explicit `LEGACY_*` literals, because the decode map
was built from the constants that just moved — left alone it would have mapped
today's spelling to itself and forgotten the vocabulary it exists to read.

The re-queue lever is one exported phrase now: clearing the status IS the re-ask,
so the messages that used to say "remove the needs-human labels" say that instead,
in one place rather than five.

Refs #1119

input.body:
Stage 3 of #1119's plan — the write-side flip. **Stacked on #1138**, so this PR's base is that branch and its diff is only the flip.

> ⚠️ **Do not merge before the gate.** The plan gates this on execution step 1: PRs 1–2 merged, `fleet-baseline` forced with `follow`, and every member's executor workflow at HEAD triggering on both ready spellings, judged from each repo's own file. Until then a member that has not taken the new stub stops seeing label events the moment the engine writes the canonical ready spelling — latency, not lost work (the hourly scheduler dispatch is the guaranteed delivery), but the plan's ordering exists to avoid even that.

## What flips

- **The constants every writer already uses now hold today's spellings** — statuses, terminals, and the origin. One edit moves every write site: the generator's occurrence wears `task:origin:planned`, a hand-created item `task:origin:ad-hoc`, a marked issue the same, and the stubs' failure issues `task:origin:github` (that one landed in PR 1). Their **names** survive because fielded pack versions import them: a pack still on the old engine writes a legacy label, which every decoder reads as what it always meant.
- **A park stops being a pair.** `needs-human` + a sub-label could be half-applied — a torn state of its own — so a park is one `task:status:needs-human-<kind>`, written by one swap. Executor, session converge, scheduler reclaim and the janitor's sweep all follow.
- **The legacy spellings become explicit `LEGACY_*` literals.** The decode map was built from the constants that just moved; left alone it would have mapped today's spelling to itself and forgotten the vocabulary it exists to read. They stay in the ensure-list too — nothing writes them, open items wear them, and deleting a label strips it from every issue that carries it.
- **The dashboard follows** with its own display key for the park column, rather than borrowing a label nothing writes.
- **The re-queue lever is one exported phrase**: clearing the status *is* the re-ask, so the five messages that said "remove the `needs-human` labels" now say that, from one home.
- **Writer-facing prose swept**: the session instructions' park table, the request worker's brief, and `writing-tasks`.

## Folders touched

```
engine/scheduler/queue/       the write constants, the one-label park, origins on
                              every born item, the shared re-queue phrase, and the
                              session/worker briefs that tell an agent what to write
packs/basics/                 the janitor's sweep writes one park label; version bumped
packs/claudinite-dashboard/   the park column gets its own display key; version bumped
packs/claudinite-growth/      writing-tasks states today's vocabulary; version bumped
```

Note on versions: `basics` and `claudinite-dashboard` are bumped **again** here (`.2`). They already moved in #1138, and `pack-version-bumped` compares against `main` — so it cannot see that these edits ride a version #1138 has already delivered. Without the second bump they would reach nobody.

## Verification

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2409 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, 67 advisory (same as `main`).

`vocabulary.test.mjs` gains the write side: every write constant is a canonical status, a park is one label, a kind word resolves to it, and the re-queue phrase names clearing the status. Seen to fail with the flip reverted. The 43 test failures the flip caused were all write-assertion churn — updated in place, and the legacy-spelling coverage now lives where it belongs, in the decode tests.

Refs #1119

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

Say the word and I will split stage 2 onto its own branch based on this one.

**PR 3 (the write-side flip) is deliberately not here**: the plan gates its merge on the fleet force that happens *after* 1–2 merge, so landing it beside them would jump that gate.

## Stage 1 — the read side + the stubs (commit `eef03a4`)

Additive on every member, in any order: **nothing writes a canonical status yet**.

- **One decode pass.** `work-item.mjs` gains the canonical vocabulary (`STATUS_*`, `ORIGIN_*`) and `statusOf` / `statusesOn` / `isParked` / `parkKindOf` / `originOf`. Every legacy spelling in DESIGN §4's table maps straight to today's, in one pass; a park whose kind cannot be decoded — an older engine's bare `needs-human`, a word a newer engine invents — reads as `failure`, the lane that holds the task's lane. No reader compares a label literally any more.
- **Transitions leave a status, not a label.** New `apply-status.mjs`: leaving a status clears *every* spelling of it, so an item filed as `task:ready` and picked up by an engine writing the canonical spelling cannot end up wearing two live statuses. The flip is then six constants changing. Side effect worth naming: a hand wake now clears the park's sub-label too, which it previously left standing.
- **The ensure-list carries the canonical labels already** — GitHub 422s an attempt to apply a label that does not exist, and the ensure pass reaches a member a converge before the flip does.
- **Both stubs, and the canon's own copies.** The executor triggers on `task:status:waiting-for-executor` *and* `task:ready` (and `task:urgent`) — a workflow's event trigger names label strings literally, so this is the one surface where both vocabularies must appear at once. Both workflows file their failure issues as `task:origin:github` + `task:status:needs-human-failure`, ensuring those labels first.

## Stage 2 — one-issue requests (commits `e2b5541`, `6e6529b`)

The shadow work item is gone. A person marks an ordinary issue `task:origin:ad-hoc`; adoption appends the machine block to **that issue's own body** and applies the first status; the lifecycle plays out where the person is already looking.

- **One lever.** Any status — live, parked or terminal — holds the mark until somebody clears it. No prior item to wait on, none to supersede; an impatient re-ask mid-run is structurally nothing.
- **Parameters ride the person's text**, not labels: `Task:`, `Model:`, `Automerge:`, beside `Blocked-by:` and `Not-before:`. Re-read at every adoption and honoured only for an author with push access, read from the collaborators-permission API — never the payload's association. An ungated ask still runs, at the defaults, and the adoption comment says so.
- **`Task: /` is new** — which task a mark asks for, defaulting to the built-in implementer. An id this repo does not carry is not adopted at all: the mark waits. Recorded as DESIGN §16.12, since §16 only sketched it.
- **Nothing closes somebody's issue.** A refusal's terminal status stands on the open issue — the run's verdict is not the issue's validity — and so does the approval park, which *is* the in-review state.
- **Identity without a title**: a marked issue's task comes from the worker path its machine block names (`taskIdFromPath`). That closed two holes — the janitor's stale-ready rule skipped every request run, and the dashboard rendered them as belonging to no task.
- **Legacy is read forever**: `claude-task` still marks (and adoption gives the issue today's origin), and a draining shadow item still writes back to the issue it names.

## Findings for the plan

- **The stubs are converge-delivered, not copied-once** — `convergeWiring` rewrites both workflow files from the vendored stubs whole. Execution step 1's contingency does not apply. The lag is that `.github/workflows/` lands as a PR somebody merges, so a member spends a window on the old copy — costing a label event, never work, since the hourly scheduler dispatch is the guaranteed delivery. That window is now a rehearsal shape.
- **`consumer-safe-change` watched only the scheduler stub.** The executor's is vendored just as verbatim and its trigger is exactly the surface a vocabulary change must carry members across, so the check (canon-local) now covers both.
- **Left out of stage 2, deliberately**: folding `add-packs` into the `Task:` field. It rewrites a cross-repo contract (the enforcer writes into members over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`), and its real failure mode needs a decision — a member whose mark label does not exist yet refuses the enforcer's write, and nothing runs, where the current dispatch-and-wake protocol is robust to that. Everything the fold needs on this side is now in place.

## Folders touched

```
engine/scheduler/queue/       the decode + apply-status; the machine block and the
                              request-side field parse; adoption rewritten to write
                              onto the marked issue; executor/converge identity and
                              the never-close rule; the built-in task and its doc
engine/scheduler/signals/     the request read accepts either mark
engine/scheduler/stubs/       both workflow stubs — the executor's dual trigger, and
.github/workflows/            the canon's own hand-maintained copies of the same two
packs/basics/                 the janitor's queue sweep decodes; do-later and
                              verify-in-production speak the mark and the body fields
packs/claudinite-dashboard/   item state, triage, parked counts and item membership
vendoring/rehearsal/          the old-workflows fixture gains the pre-#1119 executor
docs/tasks-dispatch/          DESIGN §16.12 — the `Task:` targeting field
.claudinite/local/packs/…     consumer-safe-change now watches both stubs
```

## Verification

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2409 pass, 1 fail: `engine-pack-lane-shims`, which fails on `main` too in this sandbox (shallow clone; the test refuses to walk a partial history). `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, 67 advisory — the same 67 as on `main`.

`engine-tests/scheduler/queue/vocabulary.test.mjs` (new) pins the decode table, park precedence, the mid-flip both-spellings case, the ensure-list, the stub triggers read from the real files, and the machinery reacting to canonical items — seen to fail with the source reverted. `request-mode.test.mjs` is rewritten to the one-issue model: S44 is now the one-lever guard (S49/S51 collapse into it), S47 covers the body's `Model:` and the author gate, and three new tests drive the executor end-to-end over a marked issue.

1	// The work item — the queue's one durable object (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §3, §4).
2	// An issue titled `[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task> [qualifier]`, whose labels are
3	// its state, whose body's first line is the task path, and whose optional body
4	// fields (`Not-before`, `Blocked-by`, and a request's `Request` / `Model`) are the
5	// only facts it carries beyond that.
6	//
7	// PURE, and deliberately the whole schema: everything else — anchors, guards,
8	// yields, leashes, verdicts — is computed fresh at every scheduler run and pick from the
9	// engine and the declarations at HEAD (DESIGN §14). The label-and-field vocabulary
10	// here is therefore the compatibility surface across engine versions, which is why
11	// additive change is the strongly preferred shape and a rename needs a migration.
12	//
13	// Parse/serialize of those fields lives here and nowhere else (DESIGN §9).
14	//
15	// The one import, and a frozen constant at that: the pack-rename map, which this
16	// module needs to keep reading titles written before a rename (see parseWorkItemTitle).
17	import { canonicalPackId } from '../../pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs';
18	
19	// The title prefix. Disjoint from the slot mechanism's `[claudinite-task]` on
20	// purpose: the two mechanisms coexist per-repo behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`,
21	// and neither may read the other's issues (DESIGN §14, S29).
22	export const WORK_PREFIX = '[claudinite-work]';
23	
24	// --- the canonical vocabulary (DESIGN §4, the migration of #1119) -------------
25	// Every label the machinery writes is one of three things — the item's single
26	// STATUS, its lifelong ORIGIN, or the URGENCY flag — and all of them live in the
27	// `task:` namespace. These are the spellings a reader compares against: decode
28	// first (`statusOf`, `originOf`), then compare, so an item filed by any engine
29	// version answers the same question the same way.
30	export const STATUS_PREFIX = 'task:status:';
31	export const PARK_PREFIX = `${STATUS_PREFIX}needs-human-`;
32	
33	export const STATUS_BLOCKED = `${STATUS_PREFIX}blocked`;
34	export const STATUS_READY = `${STATUS_PREFIX}waiting-for-executor`;
35	export const STATUS_RUNNING_EXECUTOR = `${STATUS_PREFIX}running-executor`;
36	export const STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT = `${STATUS_PREFIX}running-agent`;
37	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_ACTION = `${PARK_PREFIX}action`;
38	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION = `${PARK_PREFIX}decision`;
39	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL = `${PARK_PREFIX}approval`;
40	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE = `${PARK_PREFIX}failure`;
41	export const STATUS_DONE = `${STATUS_PREFIX}done`;
42	export const STATUS_REJECTED = `${STATUS_PREFIX}rejected`;
43	
44	// The four statuses an OPEN item may wear before it parks or converges. An open
45	// item wearing no decodable status at all is off the state machine — a torn label
46	// swap's leavings, which the janitor repairs (DESIGN §6.2, §11).
47	export const LIVE_STATUSES = Object.freeze([
48	  STATUS_BLOCKED, STATUS_READY, STATUS_RUNNING_EXECUTOR, STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT,
49	]);
50	// The park kinds, in the order a decoder prefers them when an item somehow wears
51	// more than one: `failure` first, because it is the conservative lane — the one
52	// that holds the task's lane rather than letting a broken task keep filing work.
53	export const PARK_KINDS = Object.freeze(['failure', 'action', 'decision', 'approval']);
54	export const PARK_STATUSES = Object.freeze(PARK_KINDS.map((k) => `${PARK_PREFIX}${k}`));
55	export const STATUS_LABELS = Object.freeze([
56	  ...LIVE_STATUSES, ...PARK_STATUSES, STATUS_DONE, STATUS_REJECTED,
57	]);
58	
59	// THE ORIGIN (DESIGN §3, decision §15.29) — who asked for this item, worn for the
60	// item's whole life beside whatever status it holds. Read here; the writers arrive
61	// with the write-side flip.
62	export const ORIGIN_PREFIX = 'task:origin:';
63	export const ORIGIN_PLANNED = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}planned`;
64	export const ORIGIN_AD_HOC = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}ad-hoc`;
65	export const ORIGIN_GITHUB = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}github`;
66	export const ORIGIN_LABELS = Object.freeze([ORIGIN_PLANNED, ORIGIN_AD_HOC, ORIGIN_GITHUB]);
67	
68	// --- the write spellings ------------------------------------------------------
69	// What this engine APPLIES. They are separate from the canonical constants above
70	// for the length of the migration only: reads decode every spelling, writes carry
71	// one, and the flip is these six values changing (#1119).
72	export const BLOCKED = 'task:blocked';
73	export const READY = 'task:ready';
74	export const URGENT = 'task:urgent';
75	export const EXECUTING = 'task:executing';
76	export const AGENT = 'task:agent';
77	export const NEEDS_HUMAN = 'needs-human';
78	
79	// @deprecated Nothing writes this since the approval park: a run that left an
80	// unmerged PR no longer CLOSES as delivered, it parks at
81	// `task:needs-human-approval` and waits to be merged. Kept exported, kept in
82	// `QUEUE_LABELS`, and still read everywhere it was read — closed issues carrying
83	// it are stored data, and a decoder that stopped recognising it would turn every
84	// historical delivered run into an un-outcomed one.
85	export const OUTCOME_DELIVERED = 'outcome:delivered';
86	
87	// @deprecated The pre-2026-08-19 spellings of the two terminals below. Kept
88	// exported so a fielded pack that imports them still loads, and READ wherever an
89	// outcome is decoded: labels are stored data on closed issues fleet-wide, so a
90	// decoder that stopped recognising these would turn every historical run into an
91	// un-outcomed one. Write `TASK_DONE` / `TASK_OBSOLETE`.
92	export const OUTCOME_DONE = 'outcome:done';
93	export const OUTCOME_OBSOLETE = 'outcome:obsolete';
94	
95	// Today's terminal spellings (DESIGN §4, §15.25): the `outcome:` namespace dissolves
96	// into `task:`, one vocabulary for the state machine's live and terminal states
97	// alike. These are what the engine WRITES; the `outcome:*` spellings above are read
98	// forever, because a closed issue keeps whatever it was closed under.
99	export const TASK_DONE = 'task:done';
100	export const TASK_OBSOLETE = 'task:obsolete';
101	
102	// @deprecated The origin marker (DESIGN §15.26). Nothing writes it and nothing
103	// branches on it: whether an item is a task's standing occurrence or an ad-hoc run
104	// is STRUCTURAL — see `isStandingItem` — so a marker that could disagree with the
105	// structure was a second authority over the same fact. Kept exported and inert
106	// because open items filed by an older engine still carry it, and a reader that
107	// choked on an unknown label would fail on exactly those.
108	export const ORIGIN_SCHEDULE = 'origin:schedule';
109	
110	// The TRIAGE SUB-LABELS. `needs-human` says an item is parked; these say what the
111	// human parked with it is expected to DO, which is the whole difference between a
112	// queue a person can skim and one they have to read. Every park wears BOTH:
113	// `needs-human` stays the single state the machine reads (every guard, sweep and
114	// dashboard already turns on it), and the sub-label is the human's routing.
115	//
116	// The four are disjoint by REMEDY, not by cause:
117	//   action   — something outside the code must change: a secret set, a scope
118	//              granted, a routine's prompt or endpoint fixed, an item re-created
119	//              with the parameter it was missing. Mechanical; no judgement.
120	//   decision — the run stopped mid-flight and what happens next is a choice:
121	//              re-queue or abandon, does the half-done work stand, was the
122	//              ceiling violation acceptable.
123	//   approval — the run SUCCEEDED and deliberately left an unmerged PR. The only
124	//              park that is not a fault; the human merges it or closes it.
125	//   failure  — the run broke: a bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a malformed or
126	//              forged item. Someone diagnoses and fixes code.
127	// `failure` is the default a park falls back to, so an unclassified park reads as
128	// "diagnose me" rather than quietly joining the mechanical lane.
